strengths: The hybrid idea is useful and intuitively motivated: syndrome-dependent learned weights retain MWPM’s structured, valid-matching output while potentially capturing correlations missed by static distance weights.

The evaluation covers two code families, independent and depolarizing noise, several code distances, and multiple classical and neural baselines. The reported logical-error-rate improvements—especially for the L=10 toric code under depolarizing noise—would be meaningful if validated rigorously.
The manuscript is generally readable, and its diagrams communicate the proposed GNN–Transformer–MWPM pipeline clearly.
The authors disclose the unfavorable dense-attention complexity rather than hiding it, and the work presents no apparent research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: the claimed “end-to-end” solution to MWPM’s non-differentiability is inaccurate. MWPM is outside training; the model is instead supervised with BCE against heuristic edge labels. Consequently, the objective does not directly optimize logical error rate or account for whether the resulting MWPM decision succeeds.

Soundness: ground-truth construction—the central supervision mechanism—is severely underspecified. “FindValidPermutation,” the timed brute-force fallback, failure handling, boundary-node construction, and selection among degenerate valid corrections are not defined. Arbitrarily choosing one representative from many equivalent corrections may also penalize other correct matchings.

Soundness: the graph definition is internally inconsistent. Section 4 alternately describes nodes as active defects and as all stabilizers, while calling the graph both complete and locally sparse. It is also unclear whether and how X- and Z-type defects may be connected, and the rotated-code inference treatment of boundaries is not specified. These ambiguities prevent verification that the produced matchings correspond to valid physical corrections.

Evidence: the paper gives no test-shot counts, confidence intervals, random seeds, train/validation/test construction, checkpoint-selection rule, or significance tests. Thresholds such as 10.95% and 17.9% are reported with unjustified precision, without finite-size-scaling fits or uncertainty estimates. Thus the plots do not support fine-grained claims such as a 0.1 percentage-point advantage over QECCT.

Evidence and reproducibility: baseline configurations and training budgets are missing, no code or generated datasets are provided, and training is described only as spanning 200–1000 epochs. There are no ablations for the GNN, global Transformer, entropy penalty, label-generation heuristic, directional maximum, or simpler learned-weight baselines, so the reported gains cannot be attributed to the claimed architectural contributions.

Significance and scalability: experiments stop at small distances (toric L≤10 and rotated L≤7) and use idealized Pauli noise with perfect syndrome measurements. There is no circuit-level noise, repeated syndrome extraction, device-correlated noise, latency, throughput, or memory measurement. Dense attention over all defect-graph edges costs O(E²); for a complete defect graph this can scale quartically in defect count and potentially as O(L⁸), directly weakening the claimed scalability and real-time relevance.

Originality: learned decoding and neural modeling of correlated syndromes are established directions. The paper does not carefully distinguish its contribution from prior neural reweighting or hybrid matching approaches, and combining a graph-attention block with a Transformer is only moderately novel absent stronger algorithmic analysis or ablation evidence.

Presentation and limitations: technical inconsistencies include h^(1) after an asserted L-layer GNN, ambiguous/double LayerNorm in Equations 19–20, and an undefined positional encoding cited to a GCN paper. Figure 5 is not convincing evidence of learning: both displayed distributions are already strongly polarized, and no quantitative relation to decoding accuracy is established. The paper also lacks a dedicated limitations discussion covering heuristic-label bias, size-specific embeddings, computational scaling, and restricted noise models. strengths: Originality/significance: Predicting syndrome-dependent edge weights while retaining MWPM as the final structured solver is a sensible hybrid direction. Combining local graph processing with global attention could be useful for correlated-noise decoding.

Presentation: The manuscript provides equations, architectural diagrams, pseudocode, and experiments on both toric and rotated surface codes. It compares against MWPM, BPOSD-2, and QECCT under independent and depolarizing noise.
The reported results are promising if valid, including lower logical error rates and estimated toric-code thresholds of 10.95% and 17.9% under independent and depolarizing noise, respectively.
The application presents no evident material ethical risk, and the paper at least discloses the GPU model used for training.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central empirical claims lack essential statistical support. The paper reports no test-shot counts, confidence intervals, error bars, random seeds, or repeated runs. It also does not explain how threshold crossings were fitted. Consequently, small differences such as 17.9% versus QECCT's 17.8% cannot be regarded as established.

The proposed objective is not end-to-end optimization of decoding, despite repeated claims to that effect. MWPM and logical failure are outside the training objective; the network merely performs supervised classification of heuristic edge labels. There is no evidence that lower edge-wise BCE correlates reliably with lower logical error rate.

Ground-truth construction is seriously under-specified and potentially unstable. It uses the simulated physical error and a logical-error oracle, iteratively permutes matchings, and sometimes invokes a timed brute-force search. The paper gives neither precise definitions nor success/failure rates, runtimes, tie-breaking rules, or label-quality analysis. Degeneracy also means that selecting one valid matching as the positive label can penalize equally valid corrections.

The actual decoder is not specified sufficiently to establish correctness. The manuscript alternates between a complete graph of active defects and feature/GNN processing over all stabilizers, while later claiming sparse GNN connectivity. It does not clearly explain how matched defect pairs are converted into physical Pauli correction paths, how X- and Z-type defects are validly paired under depolarizing noise, or how virtual boundaries are represented and decoded for the rotated code.

The comparisons are not convincing enough to attribute improvements to the proposed architecture. There are no ablations for the GNN, Transformer, entropy term, directed-edge maximum, feature set, or label-generation method. Baseline training and tuning protocols are omitted, and the MWPM/BPOSD treatment of correlated depolarizing noise is unclear, raising fairness concerns.

The scalability claim is misleading. The method constructs a complete defect graph and applies dense self-attention over its edges, with the paper itself giving O(E^2 d) complexity. Since E is already quadratic in the number of defects, this can scale extremely poorly. Parameter count alone does not demonstrate scalability, and no decoding latency, throughput, peak-memory, or large-distance experiment is provided. Polarized weights do not reduce MWPM's search space because the described algorithm does not prune edges.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or data are provided, and the paper omits training/validation/test sizes and splits, sampling counts by physical error rate, padding or batching of variable graphs, convergence/model-selection rules, baseline configurations, and several implementation details. Even the training duration is only specified as a broad 200–1000 epoch range.

Significance is limited by evaluation only under code-capacity noise with perfect syndrome measurements and small distances (toric 6–10; rotated 5–7). There is no circuit-level noise, repeated syndrome extraction, realistic device noise, cross-distance transfer, or real-time analysis. The manuscript has no meaningful limitations discussion and overstates applicability to fault-tolerant systems.

Presentation quality is below publication standard. Figures contain no uncertainty information; several running headers are clipped; page numbering is inconsistent; the bibliography begins with an authorless entry; the text cites an apparent placeholder, "goo, 2023"; some cited works appear unrelated to the claims they support; and the rotated-code construction promised in the appendix is not actually described. These issues compound the technical ambiguity.

strengths: Originality/significance: The hybrid idea—predict syndrome-dependent MWPM edge weights with local graph processing followed by global attention—is sensible and potentially useful. Retaining the classical matching stage also preserves a valuable structural inductive bias. Soundness: The reported results are promising across two code families and two noise models. On the toric code, NMWPM consistently improves over MWPM and BPOSD-2, with the largest visible gains at L=10 under depolarizing noise.

Significance: The reported toric-code thresholds of 10.95% under independent noise and 17.9% under depolarizing noise are competitive with the stated maximum-likelihood limits and slightly exceed the reproduced QECCT results.

Presentation: The main pipeline, feature construction, loss, matching transformation, and ground-truth heuristic are described in substantial detail, and the figures make the high-level approach easy to follow.
The approximately 3.9M parameter count remaining nearly constant across tested lattice sizes is an attractive property relative to the reported growth of QECCT.
weaknesses: Soundness: The paper repeatedly calls the method an “end-to-end” differentiable decoding framework, but MWPM and logical decoding success are not differentiated through. Training is ordinary edge classification against heuristic labels, so the BCE proxy is not demonstrably aligned with the central objective of minimizing logical error rate.

The ground-truth construction is heuristic and underspecified: it uses localized MWPM, searches permutations when a logical error occurs, and falls back to a timed brute-force search. The paper gives no failure rate, timeout, label ambiguity analysis, or comparison with alternative valid representatives. Because quantum errors are degenerate, forcing one selected matching as a binary target may penalize equally valid corrections.

Evaluation uncertainty is absent. The manuscript reports neither the number of Monte Carlo shots/test samples nor confidence intervals, error bars, random seeds, or variation across training runs. Consequently, small differences such as the 17.9% versus 17.8% threshold and the rotated-code improvements cannot be judged statistically convincing.

The empirical study lacks essential ablations: GNN-only versus Transformer-only, static versus learned weights, entropy regularization, node/edge features, directional-edge aggregation, and alternative ground-truth procedures. Thus, the claimed explanation that local-plus-global processing causes the gains is unsupported.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code or dataset release statement, exact training/test split, dataset size, sampling distribution over physical error rates, stopping/model-selection rule, baseline tuning protocol, or complete implementation description. The appendix additionally gives a broad 200–1000 epoch range rather than an exact setup.

Significance/scalability is overstated. Experiments stop at small distances (toric L≤10 and rotated L≤7), no decoding latency or throughput is measured, and global attention over all edges costs O(E²). Since the syndrome graph is complete, E itself is quadratic in the number of defects, potentially producing quartic scaling in defect count. A nearly constant parameter count does not establish computational scalability or real-time viability.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess: BPOSD-2 parameters and QECCT retraining details are omitted, while the plotted curves have no tabulated values. Rotated-code results reach only parity with QECCT at L=7, and threshold analysis is supplied only for the toric code.

Presentation contains technical ambiguities and inconsistencies, including whether the GNN graph contains all stabilizers or only active defects, how X/Z components and boundaries are jointly handled under depolarizing noise, and how predicted matching edges are converted into physical Pauli corrections. Some equations also have inconsistent dimensions.

Limitations and ethics: The paper has no dedicated limitations discussion and does not adequately acknowledge label bias, simulation-to-hardware transfer, measurement noise, repeated syndrome rounds, or runtime limitations. There are no evident major human-subject or societal ethical risks, but computational resources are only partially reported.

strengths: The hybrid idea is practically motivated: learned syndrome-dependent edge weights retain the robust combinatorial structure of MWPM while attempting to capture correlations missed by static weights.

The empirical scope includes toric and rotated surface codes, independent and depolarizing noise, limited circuit-level experiments, several decoder baselines, an ablation study, parameter counts, and inference-time measurements.

The reported phenomenological-noise results are promising, including toric thresholds of 17.9% under depolarizing noise and 10.95% under independent noise, plus consistent improvements over ordinary MWPM in the presented plots.

The paper is generally readable, provides useful architectural and training hyperparameters, and includes a relevant dual-use impact statement without presenting a material unresolved ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed threshold improvements are not statistically established. The paper reports no test-shot counts, confidence intervals, random-seed variation, or threshold-fitting procedure. Differences such as 17.9% versus QECCT's 17.8% cannot be interpreted as meaningful from the supplied curves alone.

Soundness/reproducibility: The decoding pipeline omits a crucial step: a matching pairs syndrome defects but does not by itself specify the physical correction path/operator, particularly on a torus with multiple homology classes. The manuscript states that the matching determines the correction without defining this mapping.

Soundness/reproducibility: Graph construction is internally unclear. Section 4 alternately defines vertices as active defects and constructs features for all stabilizers; it calls the defect graph fully connected while describing the GNN as sparse and local. The GNN equations do not show how the stated edge features enter message passing. These ambiguities prevent faithful reimplementation.

Soundness: Rotated-code boundary handling appears incomplete. A single ordinary virtual node in a perfect-matching graph can match only one defect, whereas multiple defects may independently terminate at a boundary. The manuscript neither introduces duplicated boundary nodes nor clearly specifies special PyMatching boundary semantics.

Significance/scalability: For Theta(L^2) active defects, the complete graph can have Theta(L^4) edge tokens, making the stated dense edge-level attention cost Theta(L^8). Nearly constant parameter count does not imply computational scalability, and experiments only reach distance 12. The conclusion's 'superior scalability' claim is therefore unsupported.

Originality: The advertised differentiable proxy does not differentiate through or otherwise optimize the MWPM decision. It is ordinary supervised edge-wise BCE plus entropy regularization on heuristic labels. This can still be useful, but the claimed end-to-end solution to MWPM's non-differentiability and its novelty are overstated.

Soundness: Ground-truth labels are selected as the first logically valid matching found using the simulated physical error. Because many valid matchings may correspond to the same syndrome, verified validity does not eliminate inconsistent or arbitrary supervision. Discarding timed-out hard samples also introduces training-selection bias that is not analyzed.

Soundness: Generalization claims conflate separately trained models across codes and noise models with actual cross-domain generalization. Error-rate extrapolation is demonstrated at only two points and one distance per topology; transfer learning lacks a matched randomly initialized 20-epoch control. Circuit-level evidence is limited to repetition codes at distances 3 and 5 and a rotated distance-3 experiment.

Evaluation/reproducibility: Dataset sizes and splits, evaluation sampling protocol, training seeds, baseline tuning, timing methodology, and complete source access are absent or unclear. Runtime is compared only with QECCT, not classical MWPM/BPOSD, despite claims concerning practical decoding speed.

Presentation/limitations: Figures are dense and lack uncertainty indicators; several notation and bibliographic errors remain. More importantly, there is no substantive limitations discussion covering high attention complexity, per-distance retraining, heuristic-label bias, or the very limited circuit-level setting. These evidential and specification gaps prevent reliable validation of the central claims.

strengths: The hybrid concept is sensible: predicting syndrome-dependent edge weights while retaining MWPM’s combinatorial structure could combine learned noise correlations with a valid correction mechanism.

The manuscript evaluates multiple settings, including toric and rotated surface codes, independent and depolarizing noise, limited circuit-level experiments, ablations, transfer learning, parameter counts, and runtime. The reported logical-error rates and thresholds are promising if independently validated.
The architecture and overall pipeline are presented clearly, with equations, algorithms, and diagrams. The paper also acknowledges the poor asymptotic complexity of global attention.
The impact statement recognizes the dual-use implications of fault-tolerant quantum computing. The experiments use simulated data and raise no immediate human-subject or privacy concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness: Essential decoding details are missing or problematic. A matching between defects does not itself specify the physical correction path or its homology, yet the path-selection and tie-breaking procedure is not defined. For depolarizing noise, the manuscript also does not clearly state how incompatible cross-stabilizer-type matches are prohibited. These choices directly determine logical error rates.

Soundness: The rotated-code boundary treatment appears incorrect as written. A single virtual boundary node in an ordinary perfect matching can be incident to at most one selected edge, whereas multiple defects may independently terminate at a boundary. The paper does not describe the replicated-boundary or special boundary-matching construction normally required.

Evidence: Thresholds such as 10.95%, 17.9%, and 17.7% are reported with unjustified precision. The paper gives no number of evaluation shots, confidence intervals, random-seed variation, threshold-fitting method, or uncertainty estimates. Curves from only a few small code distances cannot substantiate proximity to maximum-likelihood bounds at the stated precision.

Reproducibility: Dataset sizes, train/validation/test construction, model-selection rules, per-setting training protocol, baseline hyperparameters, and runtime measurement methodology are missing. Training is only specified as lasting 200–1000 epochs, and the repository citation provides no usable URL. The heuristic-label procedure, fallback search, correction construction, and positional encoding are not sufficiently specified to reproduce the results.

The claimed “end-to-end” differentiable framework is overstated. Training never differentiates through MWPM or optimizes logical decoding success; it applies ordinary edgewise BCE plus entropy regularization to heuristic labels derived using privileged physical-error configurations. The proposed “novel proxy loss” is therefore a standard supervised surrogate, and no evidence establishes that it is consistent with the downstream matching objective.

The ground-truth construction selects one arbitrary valid matching among many degenerate solutions and discards samples for which its search times out. Edgewise BCE penalizes other valid matchings as negatives, while the training-data filtering can bias the distribution toward easier errors. The paper reports only one filtering statistic for one setting and does not compare against matching-aware or degeneracy-aware objectives.

Significance and scalability claims are overstated. The model applies dense self-attention over the edges of a complete defect graph: with O(L^2) defects at fixed physical error rate, there can be O(L^4) edges and O(L^8) attention cost. Nearly constant parameter count and timings only through L=10 do not demonstrate scalability or practical real-time decoding.

The generalization claims conflate separately trained models with genuine transfer. Cross-topology and cross-noise results do not demonstrate that one model generalizes across those settings; the only cross-distance experiment transfers part of the network, randomly reinitializes the GNN, and fine-tunes on the target size. Circuit-level evidence is limited to repetition codes of distances 3 and 5 and one rotated distance-3 memory experiment, with the circuit noise model insufficiently documented.

Originality is limited: neural reweighting of a classical decoder, GNN/Transformer feature extraction, BCE supervision, and entropy sharpening are individually standard. The manuscript does not convincingly distinguish its formulation from prior learned decoders beyond this combination, and the most heavily advertised objective is not technically novel.

Presentation is readable at a high level but contains consequential ambiguities and errors, including inconsistent graph definitions, unclear dimensions, inconsistent method names in figures, a threshold table marked with a downward arrow although higher is better, and malformed or incomplete citations. The lengthy textbook background contrasts with the lack of space devoted to statistical methodology and implementation-critical details.

Limitations are not treated adequately. Apart from briefly stating the attention complexity, the paper does not seriously discuss heuristic-label bias, boundary handling, dependence on code size and noise model, the gap between code-capacity and fault-tolerant circuit-level decoding, or latency requirements. The ethics discussion is adequate but does not offset these technical deficiencies.

strengths: Significance: The hybrid idea is useful and practically motivated: learned, syndrome-dependent weights retain the robustness of MWPM while exploiting correlations ignored by static weights.

Soundness: Reported results are broad and consistently favorable across toric and rotated surface codes, independent and depolarizing noise, and limited circuit-level experiments. The reported toric thresholds of 17.9% and 10.95% are competitive with the cited maximum-likelihood bounds.

Presentation: The architecture, feature construction, training objective, and inference pipeline are generally explained clearly, with helpful diagrams, pseudocode, complexity analysis, ablations, transfer experiments, and runtime measurements.

Originality: Predicting matching weights with a local GNN followed by global attention is an interesting synthesis. The ground-truth construction procedure and use of learned weights inside a classical decoder provide more novelty than a fully neural decoder alone.

Analysis: Ablations examine geometric features, edge features, entropy regularization, directional aggregation, and the Transformer component. The extrapolation and cross-distance fine-tuning experiments also provide encouraging evidence beyond the headline comparison.
Ethics: The impact statement appropriately acknowledges the dual-use implications of fault-tolerant quantum computing, and no unresolved research-ethics issue is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline threshold differences are not statistically substantiated. The paper gives no evaluation-shot counts, confidence intervals, error bars, repeated-seed results, or finite-size-scaling fits. Consequently, distinctions such as 17.9% versus QECCT's 17.8%, and even the precise threshold estimates themselves, are not convincingly resolved by the evidence shown.

Soundness: Important decoding details are ambiguous or potentially incorrect. The manuscript alternates between a complete graph over active defects and features over all stabilizers; it does not clearly state whether X- and Z-type defects are matched separately or how invalid cross-type matches are excluded. It also does not specify how a matched pair is converted into a physical correction path or how toric periodic distances and homologically distinct paths are handled.

Soundness: The rotated-code treatment describes one virtual boundary node in an ordinary perfect-matching graph. A single vertex can participate in only one matched edge, whereas multiple defects may need to terminate independently at a boundary. The manuscript must explain a valid boundary construction, such as duplicated boundary vertices or PyMatching's special boundary mechanism; as written, the rotated-code algorithm and results are not reproducible.

Originality: The claimed 'novel proxy loss' is essentially supervised edge-wise binary cross-entropy plus entropy regularization. It neither differentiates through MWPM nor directly optimizes logical error, so describing the system as end-to-end optimization through a non-differentiable algorithm overstates the methodological contribution.

Reproducibility: No code or trained models are provided, and essential information is missing: training-set and test-set sizes, random seeds, checkpoint/model-selection procedure, per-code/noise training protocol, baseline hyperparameters, threshold-fitting procedure, and full circuit-noise parameters. Training is only specified as spanning a very broad 200–1000 epochs.

Evaluation: Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. It is unclear whether QECCT, BPOSD-2, and correlated MWPM received equally tuned implementations and identical samples. The particularly important correlated-MWPM baseline is plotted but barely analyzed, despite being the classical method most directly designed to exploit depolarizing correlations.

Scalability: The global Transformer attends over all defect-graph edges, giving the acknowledged O(E^2) attention cost; because a complete defect graph itself has quadratically many edges, worst-case scaling with lattice size is severe. Results only reach toric distance 12, while runtime is reported at distances 6 and 10, so the claims of superior scalability and large-distance viability are premature.

Significance: Most evidence uses idealized code-capacity noise. Circuit-level evaluation is limited to repetition codes of distances 3 and 5 and one rotated distance-3 experiment, without thresholds or comparisons to strong circuit-level decoders. This substantially limits the current practical relevance.

Presentation: Several causal interpretations are asserted rather than demonstrated—for example, that the widening performance gap is driven specifically by complementary local/global processing and that polarized probabilities reduce MWPM's search space. MWPM is still run on the graph, and no search-complexity measurement supports the latter statement.
